newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila preparing to hand defector over to Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Manila preparing to hand defector over to Seoul.

text.p: A nine-week cloak-and-dagger diplomatic saga appeared to be nearing an end on Thursday, with a South Korean official saying a top North Korean defector would leave the Philippines for Seoul next week.
Pyongyang's top ideologue, Hwang Jang-yop, defected in Beijing on February 12 and has been in the Philippines since March 18, but his exact whereabouts have remained a closely guarded secret.
President Fidel Ramos on Wednesday gave the first official hint that Hwang might leave soon when he said he was flexible enough to allow Hwang to stay a few more days.
A senior foreign ministry official in Seoul said Hwang would be in South Korea by Tuesday.

As the highest official to flee the Stalinist state, Hwang is seen by some Western officials as a man who might provide an insight into the state of mind of Pyongyang's military and government as it grapples with an economic catastrophe.
"We just don't have any access into their mindset. Maybe the defector will give us an insight," U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said last week.
South Korean media have reported that as part of its deal with Seoul to let Hwang leave, China insisted he must not be used for propaganda purposes.
North and South Korea are still locked in confrontation more than four decades after the 1950-53 Korean War ended. Chinese troops fought alongside North Koreans in the war.
The Philippine Star newspaper suggested Hwang could be a source of much valuable information.
The daily, quoting an unnamed intelligence source, said on Wednesday Hwang had sold to China top-secret blueprints for North Korean missile prototypes.
The Star quoted the unnamed source as saying a current food crisis gripping North Korea occurred "because money for basic social services has been rechannelled to the development of these missiles".
A senior Philippine military officer dismissed the report.
"If you people are printing stories like that then you might as well say that Hwang has already left the Philippines in a submarine," said the officer, asking not to be named.
The Philippine administration has astonished observers with its success in keeping Hwang's whereabouts a complete mystery.
Since he arrived, Hwang has effectively vanished.
Some analysts credited Ramos's background as former armed forces chief and intelligence officer for the success.
"Don't forget Ramos has spent a lifetime in intelligence. He is a master spy himself," political analyst Teodoro Benigno said.

Rumours and conflicting tip-offs have kept Hwang beyond the media's reach. He has been variously reported to be in the northern mountain city of Baguio, in army camps around Manila, at the former U.S. Clark air base and at the Subic Bay port.
The only officially released information was that he had been watching videos and eating Korean food.
A tip-off last week from airport officials that Hwang's name was on the manifest of a commercial plane that had just left Manila set off a scramble among reporters.
The name turned out to be that of a "Mr Wang," a suspected drug trafficker.
